newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists face job demands.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists face job demands.

text.p: France's new left-wing government faced union pressure for wage hikes on Friday as Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin made his international debut reaffirming commitment to Europe but with more stress on jobs.

The heads of the two largest unions, the pro-Socialist CFDT and the Communist-led CGT, pressed demands including a hike in the minimum wage while the new 26-strong "Pink-Green-Red" cabinet settled down to work.

And CFDT head Nicole Notat committed virtual heresy by expressing scepticism that a Socialist promise to cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss of pay would work in the fight to create jobs.
She told the daily Liberation a previous cut from 40 hours had "created zero jobs" and suspected a new cut would "have exactly the same effect."
Jospin has made the fight against record unemployment a priority and has promised to create 700,000 jobs.
Louis Viannet, head of the Communist-led CGT union, laid down his demands in an interview with Le Monde, calling for a halt to all privatisation and a big hike in the minimum wage.

Jospin avoided the squabbling by attending a congress of European centre-left parties in Sweden where he said he would keep election promises after sweeping conservative President Jacques Chirac's allies from power in Sunday's election.

But he kept the world guessing on how far he would follow up pledges to pose conditions on joining a single European currency. In a speech, he said France favoured EU construction, but with more stress on jobs.

"We are still the vanguard for the construction of a Europe that is united, generous and strong -- but not just any Europe," he said. "With high unemployment, low growth and increasing poverty, Europe can no longer be built on the back of its citizens."

Jospin has pledged no extra austerity to meet the criteria for a single currency from 1999 and to renegotiate the EU's stability pact which is meant to limit member states' budget deficits after the euro is launched.
"On the stability pact, I have no comment," he said.

The Paris stock market was up 0.5 percent in early afternoon. The market is almost five percent above its close on Friday last week, reassured by a broadly pro-European tinge to Jospin's cabinet and policies.
Jospin's cabinet, with many new young new faces and a big role for women, began outlining policies.
Transport Minister Jean-Claude Gayssot, one of three Communists in the government, stressed support for the public sector and said he would not privatise Air France or state SNCF railways.
"Nobody expects Gayssot will become the minister for privatisations, deregulation and ultra-liberalism," he said.

On the right, a member of conservative Chirac's defeated Gaullist party lent credit to leftist theories that the president had called a snap election hoping to get his allies re-elected and pre-empt sleaze probes.

Patrick Devedjian, of the Gaullist RPR, said former labour minister Jacques Barrot was threatened by a probe into party funding. Barrot and two other former Democratic Force ministers were placed under formal investigation on Wednesday.

"That is something that may have weighed on the dissolution, because if Jacques Barrot had been placed under investigation sooner, that would have led inevitably to a cabinet reshuffling, with a domino effect," Devedjian told Radio Monte Carlo.
Serge July, publisher of the daily Liberation, said that Chirac had lost much of his power when his early election gamble backfired.
"He is for the moment reduced to the situation normally reserved to the Queen of England," July wrote.
